title: There are three skilled trade job openings for every qualified worker
excerpt: The supply of skilled workers only continues to tighten as more reach retirement age amid rising demand, a Lightcast report said.
content_html:
Lara Ewen

Fri, August 28, 2026 at 3:25 AM MST 3 min read

This story was originally published on HR Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily HR Dive newsletter.

Dive Brief:

  • Skilled trades account for about 20 million jobs in the U.S., or 9% of the total workforce, according to a new report from labor market intelligence firm Lightcast — and the need for that talent only continues to increase.

  • The report defined skilled trades as 135 hands-on, in-person occupations requiring specialized education, training, certification, apprenticeship or experience but not a college degree. By that definition, there are approximately 2.1 million skilled-trade job openings every year, and about three job openings for every person who has finished a relevant training program.

  • This has created an estimated talent gap of 1.3 million workers, per the report. In seven of the 10 most in-demand skilled-trade occupations, there is already a significant labor shortage, with retirement accounting for about 40% of annual openings.

Dive Insight:

The skilled trade category has not previously been consistently defined or categorized, the report said. As a result, employers, educators, policymakers and workforce leaders have faced challenges when it came to examining sector data, identifying talent gaps and deciding how to best invest in the future of this workforce.

Meanwhile, the supply of electricians, technicians, construction workers and other skilled professionals has not kept up with the demand. In addition, more than 25% of skilled-trade workers are 55 years old or older, "suggesting demographic pressures could deepen the talent shortage," the report said.

"The impending lack of skilled trades workers has been a resounding issue in our economy for years," Ron Hetrick, principal economist at Lightcast and a contributor to the report, said in a statement. "These are people that we rely on every day to create new buildings, maintain our infrastructure, and thousands of other tasks that many of us often take for granted. [...] They're desperately needed now, but critically needed later."

The pay rate for a skilled trade job is about $13,000 more annually than the median salary for other jobs that don't require a four-year degree, the report said, adding that about one in three skilled-trade workers "move into a manager or executive role as their next occupation."

Furthermore, there's been increased demand for skilled workers due to new infrastructure investments as well as growth in the manufacturing sector and reshoring. "Data center growth alone has added a net 315,000 skilled-trade workers over the past five years," the report said.
